senses.gloss:
Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh
------------------------------------------
This is a well-known socio-cultural organization of Modern India. It is popularly known as the R.S.S. Started in A. D. 1925 by Dr. Keshav Baliram Hedgewar (A. D. 1889-1940), it aims at the च्रेअतिओन् of a non-political corps of volunteers totally dedicated to the service of the motherland, India, fondly pictured as Bhāratamātā.
It has its headquarters at Nagpur in the Maharashtra State.
Though Dr. Hedgewar was a medical doctor, he devoted all his time to building up the organization.
It was during the period of his successor, M. S. Golwalkar (A. D. 1906-1973)—more popularly known as Guruji—that the organization grew to phenomenal proportions. A saintly figure with an impeccable life, he was also instrumental in getting several other organizations started and stabilised.
The śākhā (a small local branch) is the fundamental unit of the organization with a standard pattern, routine and discipline. Great attention is paid here to physical fitness, cultivation of patriotism and high social values. It is specially impressed upon the members to look upon the whole society as one family.
The organization has undertaken several service activities. It has totally dedicated itself to offer succour and help to the country during national emergencies.
In the social field, it has taken up several programmes aimed at bringing about greater unity among the Hindus as follows: abolition of the practice of untouchability; elimination of caste animosities and forging unity among all the castes; teaching simple techniques of योग; encourage the learning of सन्स्क्रित् लन्गुअगे; reconversion into हिन्दुइस्म् of those who had left due to various reasons.
A monumental achievement of the R.S.S is the active assistance and cooperation in the construction of the Vivekānanda Temple on the Rock—now well-known as the Vivekānanda Rock—during the period A. D. 1963-1970. It is situated in the sea at the southernmost tip of India.
The organization is sustained by public contributions and contributions by the swayamsevaks (members of the R.S.S.) during the गुरुपूर्णिमा day (full-मोओन् day in the month of आषाढ, generally in July). This is called गुरुदक्षिणा celebrations.
The leaders of the R.S.S. have inspired and guided several other organizations and movements. Some of them are: विस्ह्wअ हिन्दु परिस्हद् (See VISHWA HINDU PARISHAD for details.); Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP, the largest organization of students); Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS, the largest labour movement in India); Vidya Bharati (which runs schools all over India); Vanavasi Kalyan Ashram (serving people in remote areas like forests and mountains); Sewa Bharati (conducting several service projects).
During its existence of over eighty years, the R.S.S. has faced stiff opposition as also incarceration at the hands of some sections of the society and the governments of the day. However it has successfully withstood the fiery ordeals and is growing steadily in strength.

Rasavidyā
(‘science of chemicals,’ ‘alchemy’)
------------------------------------------
Certain desires like making the physical body not only strong and healthy but also live eternally, seem to be inherent in the human psyche. So also the desire (or greed?) to convert base metals into gold.
Some sections of the scientists and doctors of ancient and medieval India seem to have believed that mercury, sulphur and mica possessed certain extraordinary qualities which were only to rediscovered. This gradually developed into a new branch of science called रसविद्या.
Gorakhnāth (11th century A. D.), नागार्जुन (6th century A. D.) and a few others were considered to be experts in this field of science.
A branch of Hindu philosophy, known as रसेश्वर दर्शन has been built round this doctrine. It propagates the theory that रस (mercury) and abhraka (mica) produced from the divine bodies of शिव and पार्वती, when mixed properly, can destroy death and poverty.
Govinda Bhagavatpāda (the गुरु of शङ्कर) has been cited as one of its ancient teachers.
This रसेश्वर दर्शन is a minor school under शैविस्म्.

Rāsalīlā
------------------------------------------
The group-dance that कृष्ण performed with the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvana is known as Rāsakrīḍā or रासलीला. It has been described in detail in the Bhāgavata (10.29-33). These five chapters are generally called Rāsapañcādhyāyī.
This important episode has been described in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (5.13,14-62) and the Harivaṁśa (Viṣṇuparva 20.18-35) also, though more briefly.
Kṛṣṇa started playing some tantalising tunes on his flute one night during autumn, sitting on the bank of the river यमुना. The मुसिच् was so enchanting that all the गोपीस् of Vṛndāvana were irresistibly drawn to him. They hurried to him and gathered round him.
As if he did not know why they had come, कृष्ण nonchalantly advised them to return to their homes, to which they refused.
Understanding their single-minded devotion and desire, कृष्ण played amorous sports with them for some time. When the गोपीस् became inebriated with pride—because they had the great कृष्ण himself for their lover—he suddenly disappeared from their midst by his inscrutable māyā power.
The गोपीस् were now smitten with intense remorse and started madly loitering in the forest region there in search of him. When they failed to trace him, they assembled in one place and started praying, pouring out the anguish that was burning their whole being. This part of the Bhāgavata (10-31) is well-known as the Gopīgītā or Gopikāgītā. It is full of the pathos of the intense pain of separation of the beloved from the lover.
Moved by their piteous cries Kṛṣna reappeared in their midst and danced the रासलीला (dance), multiplying himself to be with each of the गोपीस्. Thus spending the whole night happily with him, they, most unwillingly, returned home at daybreak.
Even though the गोपीस् had spent the whole night with कृष्ण, their husbands found them—due to his māyā—to be with them all the while! (vide Bhāgavata 10.33.38).
See also BHĀGAVATA, GOPĪGĪTĀ and KṚṢṆA.

Rasātala
(‘That which is below the earth’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata as also some of the पुराणस् contain interesting descriptions of this universe. If there are six lokas or worlds above the earth ending in सत्यलोक or ब्रह्मलोक, there are seven, below the earth also. ‘Pātāla’ is the general name given to these worlds.
The seven pātālas are: अतल, वितल, Nitala, Gabhastimān, महातल, सुतल and पाताल (Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.5.2 and 3).
According to the Bhāgavata (5.24.5) रसातल is the fourth in the series.
The Garuḍapurāṇa (15.56,57) lists रसातल as the sixth of these nether worlds.
If the various descriptions of रसातल given in these works are summarised, the following picture of this world emerges: रसातल is the fourth or the sixth of the pātālas and the abode of अनन्त or Śeṣanāga, the thousand-hooded serpent on whom Mahāviṣṇu is reclining.
Mahāviṣṇu in his Varāha (Boar) इन्चर्नतिओन् killed the demons by entering the रसातल-लोक. It was also here that he killed the demons मधु and कैटभ, taking the हयग्रीव form (with a horse’s head on a human frame).
Surabhi or कामधेनु, the celestial cow lives here with her offsprings. There is an ocean of milk here.
This world is more comfortable to live in than even Nāgaloka (world of serpents) or स्वर्ग (heaven)!

rasa
(‘that which is tasted’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most extensively used words, it has 24 different meanings and senses.
In general, it means the essence or core-part of anything.
In the darśanas (Hindu philosophical systems) it stands for the subtle element water (‘rasatanmātra’).
In the आयुर्वेद and allied health sciences, it stands for mercury.
In the culinary arts, it represents six different kinds of tastes: sweet, sour, saltish, hot (as that of pepper or chillies), bitter and astringent.
In poetics, it stands for the navarasas or nine kinds of sentiments or emotions. They are: the amorous, the heroic, the wondrous, the ridiculous, as also the sentiments of compassion, humour, fear, horror and loathesomeness.
The Taittirīyopaniṣad (2.7) calls ब्रह्मन् as रस.
